source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Informal Logic, section 4.1 (first 100k characters read)
finding: SEP credits Johnson and Blair (1977, 1994) with the ARS formulation. Acceptable premise: true, or acceptable in some other way. Relevant premise: gives some support to the conclusion. Sufficient premise set: gives enough support to warrant accepting the conclusion as likely, true or plausible.
numbers: No numbers. Dates 1977 and 1994 for Johnson and Blair.
limits: SEP does not mention Govier in connection with ARS (last 33k characters unread). Hansen (2012) argues informal logic should not assess premise acceptability at all. The page does not discuss how vague sufficiency is.
agent_relevance: S8 wording: each premise acceptable? each premise relevant to the claim? the whole set enough? Keep the three questions separate.

source: SEP Informal Logic: acceptability, uncertainty and dialogue context
finding: Acceptability is not only truth. Under uncertainty premises may only be plausible or exploratory. In persuasion dialogue a premise may need to be acceptable to the particular audience. A true premise can be unacceptable in some contexts, such as a legal hearing.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Reading of context-dependence taken from the SEP summary only.
agent_relevance: For open answers the agent needs a stated source of acceptability: given facts, common knowledge, or tool-checked. Premises that are only plausible should be marked plausible, not fact.

source: SEP Informal Logic: conductive arguments and fallacies as an alternative
finding: Sufficiency for conductive arguments means collecting enough non-decisive reasons without proving the conclusion (Johnson and Blair 2011). Fallacy lists and ARS criteria can be combined in one system. Scheme-based critical questions can replace some fallacy labels.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Possin (2016) is cited as a skeptical reply to conductive logic. Links to sibling subfields 02 (schemes) and 03 (fallacies).
agent_relevance: ARS checks can sit beside scheme questions. Fallacy names are not needed: the three failures (unacceptable, irrelevant, insufficient) give a countable defect list.

source: Johnson and Blair (2006) Logical Self-Defense; Govier (2010) A Practical Study of Argument (seen only through citations in opened papers)
finding: Both books define a good argument as one whose premises are acceptable, relevant and sufficient. Stab and Gurevych (2017) and Wachsmuth et al. (2017) cite exactly these two books for the ARS definitions.
numbers: No numbers. Books not opened.
limits: Do not quote the books from this line. Open them in a later round.
agent_relevance: Source of the three questions. Later NLP annotation guidelines reuse their wording.

source: Stab and Gurevych (2017) Recognizing insufficiently supported arguments in argumentative essays (EACL): definitions
finding: Defines ARS operationally for essays. Relevance is judged per premise against the claim. Acceptability is judged per premise (undisputed common knowledge or fact). Sufficiency is judged on the premises together. Sufficiency presupposes a non-empty set of relevant premises, but an argument with some irrelevant premises can still be sufficient.
numbers: 1,029 arguments from persuasive essays, mean 94.6 tokens and 4.5 sentences. Three trained annotators judged 433 arguments in the evaluation set.
quote: The sufficiency criterion addresses the premises of an argument together.
limits: A body paragraph is treated as one argument. Learner essays, so results may not carry to other genres.
agent_relevance: Sufficiency belongs to the premise set and can hold despite a bad premise. Verify should score the set, not only each premise.

source: Stab and Gurevych (2017): inter-annotator agreement
finding: Humans agree well on sufficiency but poorly on relevance and acceptability.
numbers: Sufficiency: 91.07% observed agreement on 433 arguments, Fleiss kappa .7672, Krippendorff alpha .7673. Relevance kappa .435 and acceptability kappa .259 (two annotators, 100 arguments).
limits: Low relevance and acceptability kappa partly come from skew: only 15% of arguments had a relevance-violating premise and 14% an acceptability-violating premise. Skew lowers kappa.
agent_relevance: Of the three ARS questions, sufficiency was the most reliably judged by people. Acceptability was the least reliable and needs an external check, not a model opinion.

source: Stab and Gurevych (2017): models for insufficient support
finding: A CNN reaches 92.5% of human accuracy at flagging insufficiently supported arguments. Lexical cues dominate: examples and personal experience mark weak support.
numbers: Human accuracy .911. Majority baseline .662. SVM bag-of-words .785 accuracy, .755 macro F1. SVM with hand features .798 and .770. CNN .843 and .827 (F1 on insufficient class .770). Top unigrams by information gain: example, my, was, instance, I, for, me, friend, he, did.
limits: Errors: 41 sufficient arguments always called insufficient (35 of them contained an example); 28 insufficient ones always called sufficient. Length alone helped little.
agent_relevance: A single example or personal anecdote is a cheap sign of weak support. A Verify rule can flag answers that rest on one example.

source: Wachsmuth et al. (2017) Computational argumentation quality assessment in natural language (EACL): taxonomy
finding: Builds a taxonomy of 15 quality dimensions. Cogency = local acceptability + local relevance + local sufficiency, sourced to Johnson and Blair, Damer and Govier. Adds global (dialectical) acceptability, relevance and sufficiency, where global sufficiency means anticipated counter-arguments are rebutted.
numbers: Dagstuhl-15512 ArgQuality corpus: 320 arguments, 304 judged argumentative by all annotators, 15 dimensions, 3 experts, 1 to 3 scale, over 14,000 assessments.
quote: An argument is cogent if it has acceptable premises that are relevant to its conclusion and that are sufficient to draw the conclusion.
limits: Debate-portal comments, not model answers.
agent_relevance: A ready checklist. The agent needs the cogency trio plus global sufficiency (are the obvious objections answered?).

source: Wachsmuth et al. (2017): score distributions
finding: Real debate arguments are mostly weak on sufficiency and almost never rebut counter-arguments, but are usually relevant.
numbers: Majority scores low/medium/high out of 304: local sufficiency 172/119/13; local relevance 25/155/124; local acceptability 84/169/51; cogency 150/131/23; global sufficiency 231/72/1; overall 152/128/24.
limits: 3-point scale, three annotators, one corpus. Global sufficiency is low because few texts contain any rebuttal.
agent_relevance: Sufficiency is the criterion most often failed. Verify should spend most effort on 'is this enough?' and on rebutting the obvious objection.

source: Wachsmuth et al. (2017): agreement and correlations
finding: Expert agreement on ARS is only moderate. Cogency and local sufficiency move together almost one to one.
numbers: Seven annotators: Krippendorff alpha at most .22. Best three annotators: alpha .23 (clarity) to .60 (credibility). Best pair: logical and dialectical dimensions above .4 except global sufficiency; overall .51; emotional appeal .26. Full agreement of three: 17.4% to 44.7%; majority agreement 87.5% to 98%. Pearson: cogency with local sufficiency .84, cogency with overall .84, reasonableness with overall .86.
limits: Alpha table was garbled in the PDF text; ranges stated in the paper text are used. Strong correlations mean the dimensions are hard to separate.
agent_relevance: Do not expect three clean independent scores for A, R and S. Use them as three prompts for finding a defect, not as scores to average.

source: Wachsmuth et al. (2017) Argumentation quality assessment: theory vs practice (ACL short): reasons and ARS
finding: Theory-based absolute ratings agree with the crowd's 'which is more convincing' pairs. Reasons people give map onto ARS dimensions, but some dimensions cannot be separated in practice.
numbers: 736 argument pairs. Kendall tau between the 'convincing' label and overall quality .64. Reason 'off-topic' correlates .95 with local and global relevance. Reason 'no credible evidence' correlates only .49 with local acceptability. Arguments with negative reasons get lower mean ratings on every dimension.
limits: Kendall values are inflated for rare labels, the authors say so. Same 304-argument base as the E17 study.
agent_relevance: People notice irrelevance very reliably (.95) and unsupported evidence less so. Relevance is the cheapest S8 check; acceptability needs a source.

source: Wachsmuth et al. (2017): crowd versus expert on theory-based quality
finding: Lay crowd workers rate ARS dimensions about as reliably as experts, but only with at least 10 ratings per item.
numbers: 10 ratings per argument, 102 workers, $0.10 per rating, 304 arguments. Crowd versus expert alpha mostly above .40 on mean ratings: local acceptability .49, local relevance .42, cogency .27, reasonableness .33, overall .43. Two independent groups of 5 gave lower and unstable values (cogency mean-rating alpha: .38 for group 1 alone, .05 for group 2 alone); about 4% answered 'cannot judge', most for global sufficiency.
limits: Cogency alpha only .27 with the crowd. Five raters were not enough.
agent_relevance: One judgment of cogency is noisy. If a model judge is used, sample it several times and aggregate in code (G4, G5).

source: Habernal and Gurevych (2016) Which argument is more convincing? (UKPConvArg1, ACL)
finding: Pairwise 'more convincing' labels from the crowd are a cheaper alternative to theory-based scoring. After cleaning they are mostly consistent with a total order.
numbers: 16,927 argument pairs over 32 topics. 1,161 crowd assignments rejected. Best-worker accuracy in a pilot .935. Cross-topic: SVM accuracy .78, Spearman .402; BLSTM accuracy .76, Spearman .354.
limits: Measures persuasion, not logical quality. Workers got no guidelines, so ARS is not measured directly. Authors skip kappa for crowdsourcing reasons.
agent_relevance: Convincing is not sound. Persuasive answers can fail ARS; Verify must not reward fluency.

source: Gretz et al. (2020) A large-scale dataset for argument quality ranking (IBM-ArgQ-Rank-30kArgs, AAAI)
finding: Point-wise quality for about 30k short arguments from binary crowd votes. In a 100-argument expert study, the gap between lowest and highest quality bins was largest for global relevance and effectiveness.
numbers: 30,497 arguments, 71 topics, 35 to 210 characters. Mean annotator reliability .12 (stance task .83). Top versus bottom bin: global relevance +0.72, effectiveness +0.64. Split-half score correlation .42 Pearson for WA and for MACE-P. An argument-length baseline did poorly.
limits: Very short arguments by design; dimension analysis used 100 arguments and 3 experts.
agent_relevance: In short texts relevance to the issue drives perceived quality. For long answers sufficiency may matter more (see essays).

source: Toledo et al. (2019) Automatic argument quality assessment: new datasets and methods (EMNLP)
finding: Builds IBM-ArgQ-14kPairs and a point-wise set with length-matched pairs to avoid length bias. Labels pass a reproducibility check.
numbers: About 14k pairs, 9.1k after filtering. Repeat annotation of a 500-pair sample gave correlation .81 between initial and repeat quality scores. In 75% of pairs the expected winner won, 84.3% when the score gap was above .5.
limits: Quality means 'would you use this in a speech', not ARS. Numbers read in one pass of the text extract.
agent_relevance: Annotator-reliability filtering and length control are needed in any ARS data we build.

source: Wachsmuth and Werner (2020) Intrinsic quality assessment of arguments (COLING)
finding: From the text alone, local sufficiency is the easiest ARS dimension to predict. Length is a strong predictor, which signals bias in the labels.
numbers: 304 arguments, 15 dimensions, leave-one-topic-out. Error for local sufficiency falls 0.39 to 0.30 (largest gain); overall 0.45 to 0.37; cogency 0.44 to 0.37. Gains not significant for four dimensions, three of them rhetorical. Human experts differ more from each other than from the model.
limits: Length is best for reasonableness and overall quality, so labels favour long arguments. Content and embedding features did badly across topics.
agent_relevance: Longer answers look more sufficient to raters. S8 needs length-normalised checks (G5).

source: Lauscher et al. (2020) Rhetoric, logic and dialectic: theory-based argument quality (COLING)
finding: GAQCorpus is a large theory-based corpus over three domains. The 15 sub-dimensions were collapsed to cogency, effectiveness, reasonableness plus overall, with the sub-dimensions as guide questions, because experts could not tell them apart.
numbers: 5,285 arguments: 2,088 community Q&A, 2,103 debate, 1,104 reviews. Five-point scale, 10 crowd votes per item. Crowd versus expert alpha at most .55. Expert-crowd alpha up to .21 for debates and up to .53 for Q&A. Pearson up to .67 (Q&A) and .42 (debates, reasonableness). A hierarchical multi-task model beat a flat one.
limits: Domain matters strongly. Sarcasm and irony drove disagreement.
agent_relevance: Four linguistics experts could not separate 15 aspects. A short checklist of 3 to 4 questions is more realistic for the agent.

source: Gurcke, Alshomary and Wachsmuth (2021) Assessing the sufficiency of arguments through conclusion generation (ArgMining)
finding: Tests whether a conclusion generated by a language model from the premises helps judge sufficiency. It does not: the premises alone carry the signal.
numbers: RoBERTa on the Stab and Gurevych data: accuracy .889, macro F1 .876 (CNN .846 and .831; human .911 and .883). Premises-only F1 .875; conclusion-only .553; generated-conclusion-only .532; premises plus conclusion best at .885 (accuracy .896). 681 of 1,029 arguments sufficient (66.2%). Manual check of 100 arguments: generated conclusions rated as likely as human ones but not unique.
limits: One corpus of learner essays. The authors say several conclusions can follow from the same premises, so re-deriving the conclusion is not a clean test.
agent_relevance: Asking a model to re-derive the conclusion is a weak sufficiency check. Test sufficiency by removing a premise or looking for a counterexample.

source: Wachsmuth et al. (2024) Argument quality assessment in the age of instruction-following LLMs (LREC-COLING)
finding: Position paper by eight authors. The main hurdles are the diversity of quality notions and the subjectivity of judging. They argue LLMs should be instructed with argumentation theory (such as cogency) and scenarios, not only fine-tuned to leaderboards. Surveys work on sufficiency, validity, acceptability.
numbers: No experiments.
limits: Opinion paper. The claim that LLMs allow more reliable assessment is a hypothesis; see the LLM study lines below.
agent_relevance: Supports prompting with explicit ARS definitions plus a scenario rather than a bare 'is this a good argument?'.

source: Mirzakhmedova et al. (2024) Are LLMs reliable argument quality annotators? Table 2: self-consistency
finding: LLMs agree with themselves far more than humans agree with each other, but consistency is not validity.
numbers: Krippendorff alpha over 3 runs: humans about .37 (novices) and .40 (experts) overall; local sufficiency .35 and .27; global sufficiency .27 and .17. GPT-3.5 on local sufficiency .69 to .79. PaLM 2 .97 to .98 without reasoning, .63 with reasoning.
limits: gpt-3.5-turbo-0613 and PaLM 2 text-bison only, no GPT-4 (cost). Same 2017 corpus of about 320 arguments.
agent_relevance: Getting the same answer on a repeat says nothing about being right (G4). Run-to-run agreement is not evidence of a correct ARS judgment.

source: Mirzakhmedova et al. (2024): agreement of LLMs with humans
finding: Agreement with human consensus is moderate overall and weakest for sufficiency. GPT-3.5 shows systematic disagreement with experts on local and global sufficiency.
numbers: Evaluated only on arguments where humans were unanimous (local sufficiency: 113 expert-unanimous, 89 novice-unanimous). PaLM 2 maximum alpha .71 (appropriateness, global relevance). Credibility range [.08, .62]. Sufficiency agreement swings even more, including negative values. Adding an LLM as extra annotator raised human agreement.
limits: Per-dimension figure values were read from a garbled figure extract, so sign and size of individual negative values are approximate.
agent_relevance: Models are weakest on the criterion Verify needs most. Treat model sufficiency judgments as hints and add checks that run code.

source: Dhole, Shu and Agichtein (2024) ConQRet: fine-grained evaluation with LLM judges (agreement on ArgQuality)
finding: A listwise GPT-4o judge with self-consistency reaches moderate agreement with experts on the ARS-taxonomy dimensions of the 2017 corpus, better than crowd workers and than earlier pointwise GPT-3.5 and PaLM 2 judges.
numbers: Alpha with experts, GPT-4o listwise plus self-consistency: cogency .47, local acceptability .45, local relevance .52, local sufficiency .57, global sufficiency .53, average .48, overall .48. Crowd: cogency .27, local sufficiency .18, global sufficiency -.17, average .36, overall .43. GPT-3.5 listwise: average .16 alone, .35 with self-consistency. Pointwise GPT-3.5 (Mirzakhmedova): cogency -.15, local sufficiency -.4.
limits: Table was extracted as text; columns aligned by matching the crowd row to the 2017 values (cogency .27, acceptability .49). Same small 320-argument corpus.
agent_relevance: Self-consistency over several samples roughly doubled GPT-3.5 agreement (.16 to .35) and a stronger model reached about .5. Supports sampling and aggregating in code, but the best agreement is still only moderate.

source: Dhole et al. (2024) ConQRet: new long-argument data and judge robustness
finding: Adds long retrieval-based arguments rated on the 14 dimensions including local and global sufficiency, and tests judges for hallucination and irrelevant context. GPT-4o judgments resisted added irrelevant context better than Gemini-1.5-Flash. Zero-shot prompting beat few-shot.
numbers: Judges tested: GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, Llama-3.x-70B, Gemini-1.5-Flash. The prompt defines local sufficiency as premises that together give enough support to make the conclusion rational to draw.
limits: Results depend on prompt wording. Detailed agreement numbers for the new data were not read.
agent_relevance: Gives a usable prompt wording for sufficiency. Judges should be tested against padding with irrelevant text.

source: Ocampo, Nyiranziza and Ceolin (2026) Argument quality assessment with LLMs: a pairwise Bradley-Terry approach (Findings of EMNLP 2026)
finding: Twelve open-weight LLMs under zero-shot, few-shot and chain-of-thought compared argument pairs for logical (cogency), rhetorical and dialectical quality. The best model, Llama-70B few-shot, reached only moderate agreement. Chain-of-thought tended to lower correlation. Small models were not clearly worse and some defaulted to one side.
numbers: Webis-ArgQuality-20: 1,271 arguments, 20 topics, 13,952 pairs. Logic, Llama-70B few-shot: Pearson .474, Spearman .479, Kendall .329, kappa .493, agreement 53.0%. Random baseline kappa .288 (35.6%); majority baseline kappa .442 (48.3%). Run-to-run label change at most 7.75%.
limits: Three-way label (A, B, tie), so chance is not 50%. The majority baseline is close to the best model on kappa, so the margin over a trivial rule is small.
agent_relevance: A 70B model barely beats a majority rule at logical quality, and chain-of-thought did not help. Fits G10 and G11: do not use written reasoning as the verifier.

source: Hahn and Oaksford (2007) The rationality of informal argumentation: a Bayesian approach to reasoning fallacies (Psychological Review 114): model
finding: A formal account of argument strength. Whether an argument from ignorance, a circular argument or a slippery slope is strong depends on content: prior belief in the conclusion, source reliability, closure of the knowledge base, and alternative explanations. The same form can be strong or weak, so form-only labels are not enough.
numbers: Reviews Oaksford and Hahn (2004), Hahn, Oaksford and Bayindir (2005; Experiment 2 N = 72) and Corner, Hahn and Oaksford (2006). New circularity studies: Experiment 1 N = 26, F(1,24) = 10.61, p = .005; Experiment 2 N = 27, F(1,25) = 64.67, p < .0001, circular argument rated 3.92 (low-alternative group) against 1.79 (high-alternative group) on a 10-point scale.
limits: Undergraduates at Cardiff rating dialogue scenarios. Mostly the authors' own experiments; no independent replication was found in this pass.
agent_relevance: Gives a graded reading of sufficiency: support is posterior belief given the premises, and depends on prior and alternatives. Verify can ask what other explanation fits the same premises.

source: Hahn and Oaksford (2007): slippery slope and strong-versus-weak arguments
finding: People's strength ratings follow the Bayesian factors. Ratings of strong examples were higher than weak ones in the last experiment, and slippery-slope strength follows the probability and prior of the consequence.
numbers: Experiment 3 (N = 40 Cardiff students): strong versus weak arguments, F(1, 39) = 72.72, MSE = 2.64.
limits: Scenario-based ratings; topic wording may affect results. Earlier experiments were reviewed, not re-derived.
agent_relevance: Strength of support is graded. A binary sufficient flag should carry a reason: what the premises rule out.

source: Boudry, Paglieri and Pigliucci (2015), cited second-hand by Habernal and Gurevych (2016) and Wachsmuth et al. (2017)
finding: Reported second-hand: normative concepts such as fallacies rarely apply to real-life arguments and are too sophisticated to operationalise. This practitioner objection motivated relative, crowd-based scoring.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Original paper not opened.
agent_relevance: Warning that rigid checklists may not fit messy real answers. Keep the checklist short and apply it only to the final claim and its support.

source: Wachsmuth et al. (2017): how the taxonomy links cogency to dialectic and rhetoric
finding: Dialectical quality builds on rhetorical, which builds on logical quality. Global sufficiency is the dialectical addition: it asks if anticipated counter-arguments are rebutted. It is the only place where ARS goes beyond a single argument.
numbers: Only 1 of 304 arguments scored high on global sufficiency by majority.
limits: Scores are for debate comments; the real rate of rebuttal in model answers is unknown.
agent_relevance: Add one open-answer S8 item: name the strongest objection and say whether the answer already addresses it. Rare in human arguments, so models may omit it too.
